title: Trusting the Machine Too Much
exam: AI and the Human Mind Project (Automation Bias)
fullPassage: Pilots trust their instruments. Physicians trust diagnostic scanners. Students trust search engines. But what happens when that trust becomes excessive? Psychologists use the term automation bias to describe the tendency to accept a machine's output simply because it originated from a machine, even when our own judgment—or the evidence right in front of us—suggests otherwise. Research dating back to the early 2000s, initially conducted in the fields of aviation and medicine, found that people frequently stop double-checking automated systems over time, interpreting the absence of an error message as proof that everything is functioning correctly. With AI chatbots now generating answers to everything from historical questions to medical concerns, researchers warn that this same bias could operate on a far larger scale than ever before. The proposed remedy is not to abandon AI altogether, but to cultivate what specialists call calibrated trust: treating an AI's response as a useful first draft rather than a final verdict, and verifying anything of genuine importance against an independent source.
